goal: Explain different staffing models for AI-native B2B sales teams.
expected_facts: The answer should describe at least two valid go-to-market staffing approaches.
It should explain how AI changes headcount needs, specialization, or support workflows.

One playbook may emphasize founder-led or product-led leverage plus AI support, while another still adds more classic sales structure once the enterprise motion hardens. The point is to match headcount design to reality, not nostalgia.

answer:
So there are two playbooks out right now for how much of a “traditional” sales team you really need at an AI B2B startup.  They aren’t mutually exclusive — most startups end up blending both approaches.  But the question is which playbook you should start with.
Playbook #1: Zero Humans Needed Here At All
The pitch here is that so long as your product is truly great, easy to deploy, and has strong word-of-mouth, you shouldn’t need any human salespeople at all. Not one. This is the pure PLG (product-led growth) approach, where customers discover your app through social media, try it themselves, and buy directly online when they see value.
And it’s working well enough for some hot new leaders.  We’ve already seen this play out at Cursor and Replit. Both Cursor and Replit let users self-deploy. Yes, they still have support and community teams.  But no real sales team. And both are worth billions and growing incredibly quickly.
In fact, Replit actually had zero sales reps until recently, despite hitting $200 million in revenue. Their founder, Amjad Masad, was literally handling every single customer call himself—including enterprise deals worth hundreds of thousands of dollars. Only after reaching $150M did they bring in their first sales hires. That’s not a typo—zero salespeople for over a year while generating eight-figure revenue.
This model requires extreme product-market fit, minimal complexity in deployment, and customers who can onboard autonomously. For high-demand products with viral components, it can be surprisingly effective.

retrieval_hits.text: So how big of a sales team do you need with a hot AI B2B startup? I think there are roughly two playbooks being run: Playbook #1: Just focusing on servicing massive in-bound demand. Many AI B2B leaders are doing this and often end up with quotas as high as $4m per AE. That sounds high and it is high, but … imagine a rep can close 2x as many deals, since they are such high intent leads. And the deal size is say $50k. So you can close 10 $50k deals a month = $500k a month bookings. $6m a year. That’s very doable at the hottest AI companies. It’s not that hard when they often have more demand than they can service. Con is you often leave a lot of prospects and leads behind. Org tends to focus mainly on top leads, as that’s plenty to hit plan. And with a small team, you can literally only do so many demos, calls, etc. These vendors are often hard to even book a call with. Playbook #2: Service every lead, go hard. I see this a lot when a hot AI B2B startup starts to hit scale, say $50m+ ARR or more. And then hire a CRO from the pre-AI world. They come in and see to hit plan … they need 100 reps. Like tomorrow. Using “old” math, let’s say the CRO brings in $700k quotas. And needs to add $150m in bookings next year, or more. You need 200 reps. Tomorrow. This ends up creating some chaos as there aren’t enough FDEs or others to support all these AEs. But it does ensure every lead gets called back, gets a demo, etc. Net net which is better? The Mega Quota? Or the Traditional Quota? I think as founders we prefer the former.

AI B2B companies do need sales teams. Almost all of them. The question is just … how large of a sales team? It’s a question no one fully questioned until recently. But now founders & CEOs are asking: - is some of the headcount better put into FDEs? We’re already seeing this - are human SDRs worth it when market demand is strong? - if AI Native B2B leaders have close rates 50% higher, does that mean they can get by with 50% fewer AEs? - many VPs of Sales and CROs now want leaner teams Net net, I’m seeing sales teams often half the size of 24 months ago They may or may not be leaving money on the table. But they are also far, far more efficient.

The 2026 Sales Org Structure
Here’s what I’m seeing work at AI-first companies:
Gone or drastically reduced:
Traditional email-based outbound SDRs (replaced by AI + 1-2 humans managing)
Inbound BDRs doing basic qualification (replaced by AI chat/voice)
CSMs who just do QBRs and don’t solve problems
Expanded:
Solutions Engineers running technical deep-dives before contracts
Forward Deployed Engineers / Implementation Specialists
GTM Engineers orchestrating AI agents
“Super SDRs” managing fleets of AI agents
Account Executives focused on complex deal navigation
New hybrid roles:
Field Data Engineers assessing integration requirements
Solutions Architects designing implementations with prospects
AI Trainers who spend 30+ days per agent getting them into production
The Bottom Line for 2026
Many AI-first B2B startups can scale to $10M, $50M, even $100M+ without a traditional sales team. But that doesn’t mean it will work for you if you have a sales-driven motion. And it doesn’t mean having humans won’t help. Maybe they are FDEs, maybe it’s a few reps. But even the hottest AI B2B startups will benefit from humans assisting PLG and managing their AI Agents. The 2026 sales team isn’t “no humans.” It’s different humans doing different things. But honestly, probably fewer humans in a traditional sales function at least.

An AI sales rep that knows the product cold 24×7 is better than struggling to hire anyone at all you trust to add to the team. The Top 10% of Sales Reps Today Close 65% of All Deals. Will We Need The Rest? Once you think about it this way, you may agree we just won’t need as many sales execs for routine deals. Even today, the top 10% of reps close 65% of deals. If AI lets you focus the human-driven deals into your Top 10% reps … you may not need all that many of the rest. Clari: The Top 10% of Reps Close 65% of Revenue. And The Bottom 50%? Just 7.6%
Enterprise Will Lag, But Change Still Coming
Enterprise sales still generally needs a quarterback to close deals. A quarterback that can manage a team and plays over many, many months. And that will require account management by humans. But also ask yourself — how many sales processes have you been through that weere great? Not that many. There will be plenty of change coming in enterprise sales with AI. But for now, it won’t be to 50/50 Human/AI ratios. We’ll see where it goes over time. You can see Windsurf’s built a massive enterprise sales team overnight. One that is AI infused, but with humans still the quarterbacks:
The Future is Already Here. Just Look. Organizations clinging to traditional sales structures especially in SMB and mid-marklet will find themselves rapidly outpaced by competitors embracing this hybrid approach. The 50/50 sales team isn’t a far-future concept—it’s the reality innovative companies are building right now.

Many AI B2B leaders are doing this and often end up with quotas as high as $4m per AE. That sounds high and it is high, but … imagine a rep can close 2x as many deals, since they are such high intent leads. And the deal size is say $50k. So you can close 10 $50k deals a month = $500k a month bookings. $6m a year. That’s very doable at the hottest AI companies. It’s not that hard when they often have more demand than they can service. Con is you often leave a lot of prospects and leads behind. Org tends to focus mainly on top leads, as that’s plenty to hit plan. And with a small team, you can literally only do so many demos, calls, etc. These vendors are often hard to even book a call with. Playbook #2: Service every lead, go hard. I see this a lot when a hot AI B2B startup starts to hit scale, say $50m+ ARR or more. And then hire a CRO from the pre-AI world. They come in and see to hit plan … they need 100 reps. Like tomorrow. Using “old” math, let’s say the CRO brings in $700k quotas. And needs to add $150m in bookings next year, or more. You need 200 reps. Tomorrow. This ends up creating some chaos as there aren’t enough FDEs or others to support all these AEs. But it does ensure every lead gets called back, gets a demo, etc. Net net which is better? The Mega Quota? Or the Traditional Quota? I think as founders we prefer the former.

[train_11725]
AI B2B companies do need sales teams. Almost all of them. The question is just … how large of a sales team? It’s a question no one fully questioned until recently. But now founders & CEOs are asking: - is some of the headcount better put into FDEs? We’re already seeing this - are human SDRs worth it when market demand is strong? - if AI Native B2B leaders have close rates 50% higher, does that mean they can get by with 50% fewer AEs? - many VPs of Sales and CROs now want leaner teams Net net, I’m seeing sales teams often half the size of 24 months ago They may or may not be leaving money on the table. But they are also far, far more efficient.

[train_665]
The 2026 Sales Org Structure
Here’s what I’m seeing work at AI-first companies:
Gone or drastically reduced:
Traditional email-based outbound SDRs (replaced by AI + 1-2 humans managing)
Inbound BDRs doing basic qualification (replaced by AI chat/voice)
CSMs who just do QBRs and don’t solve problems
Expanded:
Solutions Engineers running technical deep-dives before contracts
Forward Deployed Engineers / Implementation Specialists
GTM Engineers orchestrating AI agents
“Super SDRs” managing fleets of AI agents
Account Executives focused on complex deal navigation
New hybrid roles:
Field Data Engineers assessing integration requirements
Solutions Architects designing implementations with prospects
AI Trainers who spend 30+ days per agent getting them into production
The Bottom Line for 2026
Many AI-first B2B startups can scale to $10M, $50M, even $100M+ without a traditional sales team. But that doesn’t mean it will work for you if you have a sales-driven motion. And it doesn’t mean having humans won’t help. Maybe they are FDEs, maybe it’s a few reps. But even the hottest AI B2B startups will benefit from humans assisting PLG and managing their AI Agents. The 2026 sales team isn’t “no humans.” It’s different humans doing different things. But honestly, probably fewer humans in a traditional sales function at least.

[train_5401]
An AI sales rep that knows the product cold 24×7 is better than struggling to hire anyone at all you trust to add to the team. The Top 10% of Sales Reps Today Close 65% of All Deals. Enterprise sales still generally needs a quarterback to close deals. A quarterback that can manage a team and plays over many, many months. And that will require account management by humans. But also ask yourself — how many sales processes have you been through that weere great? Not that many. There will be plenty of change coming in enterprise sales with AI. But for now, it won’t be to 50/50 Human/AI ratios. We’ll see where it goes over time. You can see Windsurf’s built a massive enterprise sales team overnight. One that is AI infused, but with humans still the quarterbacks:
The Future is Already Here. Just Look. Organizations clinging to traditional sales structures especially in SMB and mid-marklet will find themselves rapidly outpaced by competitors embracing this hybrid approach. The 50/50 sales team isn’t a far-future concept—it’s the reality innovative companies are building right now.

retrieval_hits.text: So how big of a sales team do you need with a hot AI B2B startup? I think there are roughly two playbooks being run: Playbook #1: Just focusing on servicing massive in-bound demand. Many AI B2B leaders are doing this and often end up with quotas as high as $4m per AE. That sounds high and it is high, but … imagine a rep can close 2x as many deals, since they are such high intent leads. And the deal size is say $50k. So you can close 10 $50k deals a month = $500k a month bookings. $6m a year. That’s very doable at the hottest AI companies. It’s not that hard when they often have more demand than they can service. Con is you often leave a lot of prospects and leads behind. Org tends to focus mainly on top leads, as that’s plenty to hit plan. And with a small team, you can literally only do so many demos, calls, etc. These vendors are often hard to even book a call with. Playbook #2: Service every lead, go hard. I see this a lot when a hot AI B2B startup starts to hit scale, say $50m+ ARR or more. And then hire a CRO from the pre-AI world. They come in and see to hit plan … they need 100 reps. Like tomorrow. Using “old” math, let’s say the CRO brings in $700k quotas. And needs to add $150m in bookings next year, or more. You need 200 reps. Tomorrow. This ends up creating some chaos as there aren’t enough FDEs or others to support all these AEs. But it does ensure every lead gets called back, gets a demo, etc. Net net which is better? The Mega Quota? Or the Traditional Quota? I think as founders we prefer the former.

AI B2B companies do need sales teams. Almost all of them. The question is just … how large of a sales team? It’s a question no one fully questioned until recently. But now founders & CEOs are asking: - is some of the headcount better put into FDEs? We’re already seeing this - are human SDRs worth it when market demand is strong? - if AI Native B2B leaders have close rates 50% higher, does that mean they can get by with 50% fewer AEs? - many VPs of Sales and CROs now want leaner teams Net net, I’m seeing sales teams often half the size of 24 months ago They may or may not be leaving money on the table. But they are also far, far more efficient.

The 2026 Sales Org Structure
Here’s what I’m seeing work at AI-first companies:
Gone or drastically reduced:
Traditional email-based outbound SDRs (replaced by AI + 1-2 humans managing)
Inbound BDRs doing basic qualification (replaced by AI chat/voice)
CSMs who just do QBRs and don’t solve problems
Expanded:
Solutions Engineers running technical deep-dives before contracts
Forward Deployed Engineers / Implementation Specialists
GTM Engineers orchestrating AI agents
“Super SDRs” managing fleets of AI agents
Account Executives focused on complex deal navigation
New hybrid roles:
Field Data Engineers assessing integration requirements
Solutions Architects designing implementations with prospects
AI Trainers who spend 30+ days per agent getting them into production
The Bottom Line for 2026
Many AI-first B2B startups can scale to $10M, $50M, even $100M+ without a traditional sales team. But that doesn’t mean it will work for you if you have a sales-driven motion. And it doesn’t mean having humans won’t help. Maybe they are FDEs, maybe it’s a few reps. But even the hottest AI B2B startups will benefit from humans assisting PLG and managing their AI Agents. The 2026 sales team isn’t “no humans.” It’s different humans doing different things. But honestly, probably fewer humans in a traditional sales function at least.

An AI sales rep that knows the product cold 24×7 is better than struggling to hire anyone at all you trust to add to the team. The Top 10% of Sales Reps Today Close 65% of All Deals. Will We Need The Rest? Once you think about it this way, you may agree we just won’t need as many sales execs for routine deals. Even today, the top 10% of reps close 65% of deals. If AI lets you focus the human-driven deals into your Top 10% reps … you may not need all that many of the rest. Clari: The Top 10% of Reps Close 65% of Revenue. And The Bottom 50%? Just 7.6%
Enterprise Will Lag, But Change Still Coming
Enterprise sales still generally needs a quarterback to close deals. A quarterback that can manage a team and plays over many, many months. And that will require account management by humans. But also ask yourself — how many sales processes have you been through that weere great? Not that many. There will be plenty of change coming in enterprise sales with AI. But for now, it won’t be to 50/50 Human/AI ratios. We’ll see where it goes over time. You can see Windsurf’s built a massive enterprise sales team overnight. One that is AI infused, but with humans still the quarterbacks:
The Future is Already Here. Just Look. Organizations clinging to traditional sales structures especially in SMB and mid-marklet will find themselves rapidly outpaced by competitors embracing this hybrid approach. The 50/50 sales team isn’t a far-future concept—it’s the reality innovative companies are building right now.

Topic: How Big of a Sales Team Do You Really Need at a Hot AI B2B Startup? The Two Playbooks.

Source passages:
[train_11587]
So how big of a sales team do you need with a hot AI B2B startup? I think there are roughly two playbooks being run: Playbook #1: Just focusing on servicing massive in-bound demand. Many AI B2B leaders are doing this and often end up with quotas as high as $4m per AE. That sounds high and it is high, but … imagine a rep can close 2x as many deals, since they are such high intent leads. And the deal size is say $50k. So you can close 10 $50k deals a month = $500k a month bookings. $6m a year. That’s very doable at the hottest AI companies. It’s not that hard when they often have more demand than they can service. Con is you often leave a lot of prospects and leads behind. Org tends to focus mainly on top leads, as that’s plenty to hit plan. And with a small team, you can literally only do so many demos, calls, etc. These vendors are often hard to even book a call with. Playbook #2: Service every lead, go hard. I see this a lot when a hot AI B2B startup starts to hit scale, say $50m+ ARR or more. And then hire a CRO from the pre-AI world. They come in and see to hit plan … they need 100 reps. Like tomorrow. Using “old” math, let’s say the CRO brings in $700k quotas. And needs to add $150m in bookings next year, or more. You need 200 reps. Tomorrow. This ends up creating some chaos as there aren’t enough FDEs or others to support all these AEs. But it does ensure every lead gets called back, gets a demo, etc. Net net which is better? The Mega Quota? Or the Traditional Quota? I think as founders we prefer the former.

[train_11725]
AI B2B companies do need sales teams. Almost all of them. The question is just … how large of a sales team? It’s a question no one fully questioned until recently. But now founders & CEOs are asking: - is some of the headcount better put into FDEs? We’re already seeing this - are human SDRs worth it when market demand is strong? - if AI Native B2B leaders have close rates 50% higher, does that mean they can get by with 50% fewer AEs? - many VPs of Sales and CROs now want leaner teams Net net, I’m seeing sales teams often half the size of 24 months ago They may or may not be leaving money on the table. But they are also far, far more efficient.

[train_665]
The 2026 Sales Org Structure
Here’s what I’m seeing work at AI-first companies:
Gone or drastically reduced:
Traditional email-based outbound SDRs (replaced by AI + 1-2 humans managing)
Inbound BDRs doing basic qualification (replaced by AI chat/voice)
CSMs who just do QBRs and don’t solve problems
Expanded:
Solutions Engineers running technical deep-dives before contracts
Forward Deployed Engineers / Implementation Specialists
GTM Engineers orchestrating AI agents
“Super SDRs” managing fleets of AI agents
Account Executives focused on complex deal navigation
New hybrid roles:
Field Data Engineers assessing integration requirements
Solutions Architects designing implementations with prospects
AI Trainers who spend 30+ days per agent getting them into production
The Bottom Line for 2026
Many AI-first B2B startups can scale to $10M, $50M, even $100M+ without a traditional sales team. But that doesn’t mean it will work for you if you have a sales-driven motion. And it doesn’t mean having humans won’t help. Maybe they are FDEs, maybe it’s a few reps. But even the hottest AI B2B startups will benefit from humans assisting PLG and managing their AI Agents. The 2026 sales team isn’t “no humans.” It’s different humans doing different things. But honestly, probably fewer humans in a traditional sales function at least.

[train_5401]
An AI sales rep that knows the product cold 24×7 is better than struggling to hire anyone at all you trust to add to the team. The Top 10% of Sales Reps Today Close 65% of All Deals. Will We Need The Rest? Once you think about it this way, you may agree we just won’t need as many sales execs for routine deals. Even today, the top 10% of reps close 65% of deals. If AI lets you focus the human-driven deals into your Top 10% reps … you may not need all that many of the rest. Clari: The Top 10% of Reps Close 65% of Revenue. And The Bottom 50%? Just 7.6%
Enterprise Will Lag, But Change Still Coming
Enterprise sales still generally needs a quarterback to close deals. A quarterback that can manage a team and plays over many, many months. And that will require account management by humans. But also ask yourself — how many sales processes have you been through that weere great? Not that many. There will be plenty of change coming in enterprise sales with AI. But for now, it won’t be to 50/50 Human/AI ratios. We’ll see where it goes over time. You can see Windsurf’s built a massive enterprise sales team overnight. One that is AI infused, but with humans still the quarterbacks:
The Future is Already Here. Just Look. Organizations clinging to traditional sales structures especially in SMB and mid-marklet will find themselves rapidly outpaced by competitors embracing this hybrid approach. The 50/50 sales team isn’t a far-future concept—it’s the reality innovative companies are building right now.

Con is you often leave a lot of prospects and leads behind. Org tends to focus mainly on top leads, as that’s plenty to hit plan. And with a small team, you can literally only do so many demos, calls, etc. These vendors are often hard to even book a call with. Playbook #2: Service every lead, go hard. I see this a lot when a hot AI B2B startup starts to hit scale, say $50m+ ARR or more. And then hire a CRO from the pre-AI world. They come in and see to hit plan … they need 100 reps. Like tomorrow. Using “old” math, let’s say the CRO brings in $700k quotas. And needs to add $150m in bookings next year, or more. You need 200 reps. Tomorrow. This ends up creating some chaos as there aren’t enough FDEs or others to support all these AEs. But it does ensure every lead gets called back, gets a demo, etc. Net net which is better? The Mega Quota? Or the Traditional Quota? I think as founders we prefer the former.

AI B2B companies do need sales teams. Almost all of them. The question is just … how large of a sales team? It’s a question no one fully questioned until recently. CSMs who just do QBRs and don’t solve problems

“Super SDRs” managing fleets of AI agents

AI Trainers who spend 30+ days per agent getting them into production

So how big of a sales team do you need with a hot AI B2B startup? I think there are roughly two playbooks being run: Playbook #1: Just focusing on servicing massive in-bound demand. Many AI B2B leaders are doing this and often end up with quotas as high as $4m per AE. That sounds high and it is high, but … imagine a rep can close 2x as many deals, since they are such high intent leads. And the deal size is say $50k. So you can close 10 $50k deals a month = $500k a month bookings. $6m a year. That’s very doable at the hottest AI companies. It’s not that hard when they often have more demand than they can service. Con is you often leave a lot of prospects and leads behind. Org tends to focus mainly on top leads, as that’s plenty to hit plan. And with a small team, you can literally only do so many demos, calls, etc. These vendors are often hard to even book a call with. Playbook #2: Service every lead, go hard. I see this a lot when a hot AI B2B startup starts to hit scale, say $50m+ ARR or more. And then hire a CRO from the pre-AI world. They come in and see to hit plan … they need 100 reps. Like tomorrow. Using “old” math, let’s say the CRO brings in $700k quotas. And needs to add $150m in bookings next year, or more. You need 200 reps. Tomorrow. This ends up creating some chaos as there aren’t enough FDEs or others to support all these AEs. But it does ensure every lead gets called back, gets a demo, etc. Net net which is better? The Mega Quota? Or the Traditional Quota? I think as founders we prefer the former.

[train_11725]
AI B2B companies do need sales teams. Almost all of them. The question is just … how large of a sales team? It’s a question no one fully questioned until recently. But now founders & CEOs are asking: - is some of the headcount better put into FDEs? We’re already seeing this - are human SDRs worth it when market demand is strong? - if AI Native B2B leaders have close rates 50% higher, does that mean they can get by with 50% fewer AEs? - many VPs of Sales and CROs now want leaner teams Net net, I’m seeing sales teams often half the size of 24 months ago They may or may not be leaving money on the table. But they are also far, far more efficient.

[train_665]
The 2026 Sales Org Structure
Here’s what I’m seeing work at AI-first companies:
Gone or drastically reduced:
Traditional email-based outbound SDRs (replaced by AI + 1-2 humans managing)
Inbound BDRs doing basic qualification (replaced by AI chat/voice)
CSMs who just do QBRs and don’t solve problems
Expanded:
Solutions Engineers running technical deep-dives before contracts
Forward Deployed Engineers / Implementation Specialists
GTM Engineers orchestrating AI agents
“Super SDRs” managing fleets of AI agents
Account Executives focused on complex deal navigation
New hybrid roles:
Field Data Engineers assessing integration requirements
Solutions Architects designing implementations with prospects
AI Trainers who spend 30+ days per agent getting them into production

Many AI-first B2B startups can scale to $10M, $50M, even $100M+ without a traditional sales team. But that doesn’t mean it will work for you if you have a sales-driven motion. Enterprise sales still generally needs a quarterback to close deals. A quarterback that can manage a team and plays over many, many months. And that will require account management by humans. But also ask yourself — how many sales processes have you been through that weere great? Not that many. There will be plenty of change coming in enterprise sales with AI. But for now, it won’t be to 50/50 Human/AI ratios. We’ll see where it goes over time. You can see Windsurf’s built a massive enterprise sales team overnight. One that is AI infused, but with humans still the quarterbacks:
The Future is Already Here. Just Look. Organizations clinging to traditional sales structures especially in SMB and mid-marklet will find themselves rapidly outpaced by competitors embracing this hybrid approach. The 50/50 sales team isn’t a far-future concept—it’s the reality innovative companies are building right now.

answer:
SaaS isn’t dead.  Not yet.  And even if it was … well, you can see folks like Salesforce doing better these days as well.  But what I do think is clear is there hasn’t been much change in how many of us sell software since 2010/2011:
The products got more powerful over time, and the teams grew bigger
But basically, they were still selling the same way for years
I’m not sure any of us truly adapted to the changes of the past few years.  We’re finally seeing some real adaptations in early 2024 though.  It’s starting to get exciting.  Here’s my take on where things stand today:
It used to be easy to win in SaaS with high NRR and happy customers
We’d close them in the early days, then raise prices every year because the product got better and better.  Today, NRR overall has fallen to 105%.   And in fact, in the public companies, their net retention has fallen below 100% on average.  Even ZoomInfo had negative NRR!  This means churn has gone up and up.  Folks aren’t staying as long anymore.  It’s harder to keep customers when competition gets hotter, especially in the age of AI.  So we’ve entered a new era where we don’t have 130%+ NRR and happy customers buying more and more seats each year.  Instead, we often struggle to retain our existing base, and lose them once they buy another app that does something similar.  It’s tough out there.  But the best are finding a way.
We used to use prototypes to try to get deals done quickly
A great tool!  In the Age of AI, now you can build prototypes almost instantly.  In fact, one of the most recent tools we tried here at SaaStr took less than 24 hours to deploy (!).

SaaS isn’t dead, even with the massive sell off this year (and really since July 2025)

But … what is dead is the classic pattern and way to scale:

- 1, maybe 2 players, take over a space by $20m ARR
- Massive sales & marketing spend gets you to $100m+ ARR, often takes years
- Product then mostly stagnant, quarterly releases,  big platform advance only every 5 years or so
- High NRR of 130%+ in enterprise, 110%+ in SMBs basically on autopilot
- Customers happily renew and keep spending more with you

That is dead

It’s been replaced with:

- Prototype built in days
- AI creating 100s of new competitors, many dramatically better at agentic functionality 
- Outliers get to $100m in 12 months, become budget magnets
- AI radically expanding functionality, obliterating prior pace software development 
- Massive reluctance to buy more products or seats from slow moving vendors they already pay for 
- High reluctance to contribute any budget that doesn’t show massive ROI almost immediately (from AI)
- Endless price increases since 2022 leading to frustration and even anger at existing leaders and brands

That is "SaaS" today.  If you want to win.

The Era of Slow SaaS Evolution is Dead
SaaS and B2B software is experiencing an unprecedented transformation. From 2011 to 2023, the SaaS world was … predictable. You’d build a product, add a couple features annually, make quarterly releases, and if you hit $10M ARR with 110-120% net retention, your ticket was pretty much punched to $100m+ ARR and beyond. But that playbook is now obsolete. Revenue is still recurring in SaaS, of course. But the rate of change, and the threats from AI, are making the model far tougher than it was just 12 months ago. The stable, predictable SaaS world we knew has been replaced by rapid AI-driven evolution that’s breaking all the old rules. What worked yesterday is aging out FAST. The truth is harsh but necessary:
if you’re still running your 2023 playbook in 2025, you’re already falling behind. The 4 Red Flags You’re Getting “Maimed” by AI-First Competitors
You might not see competitors taking all your business overnight, but the “death by a thousand cuts” has begun:
Deals are getting smaller
Net Retention is steadily declining
Win rates dropping by 10-15%
(from 90% to 78%)
Existing customers downgrading
This isn’t about total displacement (yet). It’s about getting “maimed” as innovative AI-first companies eat into your business—not by destroying you, but by steadily cutting away at your growth.

So it was just 8 months ago
we wrote “Is SaaS Dead?
” and the post not only took off, it summarized a zeitgeist, a malaise, a feeling across much of B2B at the start of 2024. That SaaS was Dead. A combination of AI and buyer retrenchment had killed it. What a difference 8 months makes. It’s not 2021 again, but so much has changed for the better as the year ends:
Many top SaaS and Cloud stocks are up +40%-60% or more in the back half of the yea
r. Not all of them, but so many. This makes everyone feel … richer. They are richer. Many top SaaS and Cloud leaders have seen growth re-accelerate
. This is a bigger deal. Shopify is growing far faster today at $9B ARR (a stunning 26%) than it was just a year before (21%). Even folks that were struggling to rebound from pandemic-fueled growth like Twilio have bounced back, to an extent at least. Twilio is now above 10% growth again. This isn’t 2020 levels of growth, but acceleration is acceleration. Many SaaS leaders are now benefitting from selling AI
. Salesforce has seen a boost. Dialpad has seen
stunning re-acceleration, from $200m ARR last year to $300m+ this year
. Not everyone has benefitted from selling AI to their base. But a number have. IPOs are restarting — and really good ones are coming
. There have only been 4 SaaS IPOs since 2021, but they’ve done well, and ServiceTitan had a big pop in its recent IPO. The pipeline looks strong for the back half of 2025 and into 2026, from Canva to Databricks to Stripe to Wiz to Snyk and on and on. More liquidity makes everyone feel better, for many reasons.
New!!  There Probably Is No Downturn in SaaS. It’s Time To Stop Waiting For It To End.

- Massive sales & marketing spend gets you to $100m+ ARR, often takes years

- Customers happily renew and keep spending more with you

- Prototype built in days
- AI creating 100s of new competitors, many dramatically better at agentic functionality 
- Outliers get to $100m in 12 months, become budget magnets
- AI radically expanding functionality, obliterating prior pace software development 
- Massive reluctance to buy more products or seats from slow moving vendors they already pay for

- Endless price increases since 2022 leading to frustration and even anger at existing leaders and brands

if you’re still running your 2023 playbook in 2025, you’re already falling behind. The 4 Red Flags You’re Getting “Maimed” by AI-First Competitors

Deals are getting smaller
Net Retention is steadily declining
Win rates dropping by 10-15%

SaaS isn’t dead, even with the massive sell off this year (and really since July 2025)

But … what is dead is the classic pattern and way to scale:

- 1, maybe 2 players, take over a space by $20m ARR
- Massive sales & marketing spend gets you to $100m+ ARR, often takes years
- Product then mostly stagnant, quarterly releases,  big platform advance only every 5 years or so
- High NRR of 130%+ in enterprise, 110%+ in SMBs basically on autopilot
- Customers happily renew and keep spending more with you

That is dead

It’s been replaced with:

- Prototype built in days
- AI creating 100s of new competitors, many dramatically better at agentic functionality 
- Outliers get to $100m in 12 months, become budget magnets
- AI radically expanding functionality, obliterating prior pace software development 
- Massive reluctance to buy more products or seats from slow moving vendors they already pay for 
- High reluctance to contribute any budget that doesn’t show massive ROI almost immediately (from AI)
- Endless price increases since 2022 leading to frustration and even anger at existing leaders and brands

That is "SaaS" today.  If you want to win.

The Era of Slow SaaS Evolution is Dead
SaaS and B2B software is experiencing an unprecedented transformation. From 2011 to 2023, the SaaS world was … predictable. You’d build a product, add a couple features annually, make quarterly releases, and if you hit $10M ARR with 110-120% net retention, your ticket was pretty much punched to $100m+ ARR and beyond. But that playbook is now obsolete. Revenue is still recurring in SaaS, of course. But the rate of change, and the threats from AI, are making the model far tougher than it was just 12 months ago. The stable, predictable SaaS world we knew has been replaced by rapid AI-driven evolution that’s breaking all the old rules. What worked yesterday is aging out FAST. The truth is harsh but necessary:
if you’re still running your 2023 playbook in 2025, you’re already falling behind. The 4 Red Flags You’re Getting “Maimed” by AI-First Competitors

Deals are getting smaller
Net Retention is steadily declining
Win rates dropping by 10-15%
(from 90% to 78%)
Existing customers downgrading
This isn’t about total displacement (yet). It’s about getting “maimed” as innovative AI-first companies eat into your business—not by destroying you, but by steadily cutting away at your growth.
